title: Penrose diary — 3 September 1932
---

3 September 1932.

A typhoon struck last night. Before dusk an old woman and three fishermen came to the keeper's house and begged me to leave the lamp dark. They believe that a light burning in a storm calls the drowned home, and that the living who follow it walk into the sea and never come back. I told them, as an engineer, that a lighthouse dark in a storm is a lighthouse that drowns ships. I lit it myself.

Near midnight a boy of perhaps ten, a fisherman's son, was seen walking along the sea wall toward the cliff, following the beam. We searched until the water drove us off. He has not been found.

Searching the tide room, I was caught by the returning flood and had to wade out chest-deep. My silver watch filled with sea water; it stopped at 3:47 and will not start again. I have hung it on a nail above the high-water line in that room, where the boy's mother can see it if she ever goes down. I will not take it home.

Let the record show: the keeper is instructed that the light shall not burn during a typhoon. I was wrong, and the village was right, whatever the reason.
